ordered_diagnoses: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries

s1.syndrome_frame: Progressive dyspnea on exertion with cardiac and oncologic history
salient_findings: ST elevation in leads V1, V2, and V3 with T-wave inversions
key_facts: Patient is a man in his 70s
History of multiple prior cardiac events
History of lung cancer with metastatic disease to the brain and myocardium
Received 2 drug-eluting stents to the right coronary artery 10 months prior
Denies chest pain at presentation
High-sensitivity cardiac troponin-T level was 40 ng/L
ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute
ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1, V2, and V3
Transthoracic echocardiogram shows well-circumscribed mass in the left ventricular mid-apical anteroseptum
Large pericardial effusion with signs of impending cardiac tamponade
Preserved left ventricular systolic function
No regional wall motion abnormalities

raw.rationale: The patient has a history of lung cancer with metastatic disease to the brain and myocardium, and the transthoracic echocardiogram shows a well-circumscribed mass in the left ventricular mid-apical anteroseptum, which is consistent with cardiac metastasis.

rejected.label: Cardiac tamponade
rejected.why: Although there is a large pericardial effusion with signs of impending cardiac tamponade, this is more likely a consequence of the cardiac metastasis rather than the primary diagnosis.

rejected.label: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries
rejected.why: The coronary angiography shows nonobstructive epicardial coronary artery disease without evidence of acute thrombotic or embolic occlusion, making myocardial infarction less likely.

rejected.label: Constrictive pericarditis
rejected.why: There is no evidence of pericardial thickening or calcification, and the patient's symptoms and imaging findings are more consistent with cardiac metastasis.

rejected.label: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
rejected.why: The patient's preserved left ventricular systolic function and lack of regional wall motion abnormalities make restrictive cardiomyopathy less likely.
